coverage.assessment: Three cuts loosen connections. The gratified-spectator clause before V3 is gone. Hay's England-first combine and Chamberlain's embarrassment are gone, so 'fretting him in practical forms' is unsupported. The 'drifted as attraction' line, which seeds the closing attraction formula, is also cut.
'The change' in p1 now lacks its stated antecedent, England learning its lesson. Elsewhere 'Hay shouldered his pack' is helpfully clarified, and entrances, exits and locations are clear.

Hay's speech is still quoted, attributed and ends on the rhetorical question. Its condensation drops the six-weeks/one-vote fact and the Constitution line, leaving the opening norm without its counterpoint. The 'Adams, you reason too much!' reproach is kept.

The required qualifications hold. The epitaph is labelled satire and credited to Maine and Sohm. Office-as-poison is kept 'in his fancy'. 'At cost of life' remains Hay's own foreboding. All six dates are intact.
There is no premature disclosure of Hay's death. The retrospective irony of the 1874 Assistant Professor and the third-person distance are maintained.

Long periodic sentences and the dash accumulation of V5 survive. Some self-deprecating closers are cut ('as ignorant as an astronomer', 'deplorably Bostonian', 'bent on crushing rivalry'), as is Adams's measure of his debt to La Farge. This is a defensible cost.
The Whistler anecdote loses its art-versus-talk premise and the fact that La Farge agreed. As a result, 'difference of expression' no longer clearly means shared opinion differently expressed.
All eight dependencies are intact at both endpoints in the actual revised texts. Chapter 025 is omitted, but the local ambassador gloss covers the gap.

findings.claim: The revision cuts the sentence in which England learns its lesson just as Hay would have faced old anxieties. The next sentence's 'the change' now follows only 'the blessing fell on Hay'. The change is named only afterwards, in the Germany sentence.
findings.counterevidence: V1 in the following sentence ('frightened England into America's arms') supplies the referent soon after.

findings.reader_effect: The reader must infer what changed. The irony of timing ('just at the moment') that makes the blessing 'pure chance' is also lost.
findings.title: 'The change' loses its antecedent after England's lesson is cut

findings.claim: In the source, 'After all, friends had done the work' justifies feeling as gratified as if one had shared the danger instead of 'looking on from a great distance'. The revision cuts that clause, so 'After all' now follows bare acquiescence.

findings.claim: The first draft kept two links between the Boer War and Hay's problem. One is Chamberlain's attitude being 'terribly embarrassing to Hay'. The other is Hay's need to bring England first into the combine while Germany, Russia and France combined against England, helped by the Boer War. The revision deletes both.
findings.counterevidence: Pauncefote as Hay's sole ally is kept, and 'abroad whatever helped on one side' still gestures at the problem.

evidence.quote: Hay thought England must be brought first into the combine; but at that time Germany, Russia, and France were all combining against England, and the Boer War helped them.
To him the attitude of Mr. Chamberlain and his colleagues seemed exceedingly un-American, and terribly embarrassing to Hay.
Hay thought England must be brought first into the combine
he would not bother Hay with theoretical objections which were every day fretting him in practical forms
At home, interests could be easily combined by simply paying their price; but abroad whatever helped on one side, hurt him on another.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the 'Hay thought England must be brought first into the combine...' sentence in p21. Optionally add 'and terribly embarrassing to Hay' at the end of p18.
findings.plan_relation: The essential section on the Boer War, McKinley's pool and Hay depends on this link.
findings.reader_effect: The Boer War now reads only as Adams's private outrage. The reader loses why his objections were 'every day fretting' Hay 'in practical forms', and why helping one side abroad hurt on another and left only Pauncefote as an ally.
findings.title: Boer War cut loose from Hay's diplomatic difficulty

The self-deprecating closers 'as ignorant as an astronomer', 'deplorably Bostonian' and 'He seemed bent on crushing rivalry' are also cut.

strengths: All eight protected verbatim passages survive intact, including the dash accumulation of V5 and the paradox of V6.
The Latin epitaph is kept in full, presented as satire and credited to Maine and Sohm.
The Surrenden telegram keeps its Armada/Elizabeth framing and the hinge to Hay's summons in a single sentence.
The close keeps Langley's doubting temper, Stallo, 'Adams read and failed to understand' and the Rasselas/Trocadero ending on May 12.
summary: The revision keeps every planned verbatim line, all dated events, the Hay gloss, the Sac and Soc satire with credit to Maine and Sohm, Hay's quoted Senate speech, the s = gt^2/2 joke and Stallo. All eight dependencies survive. There are no blockers. The remaining problems come from cuts made in this revision that the first draft had avoided. The revision drops the clauses that anchor 'the change' and 'After all'. It removes the Boer War's link to Hay's diplomacy. It cuts the fact that gives Hay's opening treaty sentence its sting. It weakens the premise and logic of the Whistler dinner. Some self-mocking voice and attraction foreshadowing is also thinned.
